en: Though he knew the incomparable suffering of birth and was capable of attaining peace himself,
out of compassion for the sake of calming sentient beings, he wandered through many eons;
and having renounced the great bliss of peace within himself, he taught the Dharma to others.
Homage to that Buddha, the omniscient one, for whom all migrations have ceased;
he who, while beings wander through the worlds day after day, does not return; he whose nature is the cessation of becoming, who neither arises nor perishes within the course of existence.
Homage to that Great Dharma, through the complete exhaustion of all afflictions, in which there is no birth, no death, no diseases, and no mental agonies;
to him who is free from doubt and unshakable regarding the world’s disputes over its origin and its end.
Having realized for himself that arising is caused by craving, and that through the destruction of craving there is nirvana;

established in both the path and its fruit as an unsurpassed field of merit, possessing the conduct [of the noble ones]—homage to that Saṅgha, the most worthy of worship in the world, a treasury of merit. (26.1.3)

Those who perceive the gradual realization [of the truths], the state of existence, and the transition [at death] even while beings reside in the heavens; who see the practice of Dharma established throughout the three times; and who see that the first dhyāna is not present in the fruit, nor is the purity of the mind merely ordinary—[they are the wise].
I pay homage to those teachers of the Sarvāstivāda, who are experts in the yoga of the ultimate truth;

who, through the power of the yoga of correct practice, shall attain the destruction of suffering; who delight in selflessness, are skilled in the noble path, and are adorned with the faculty of wisdom.
I pay homage to those sons of the Buddha and to the Śrāvakas who, through wisdom, perceive this world as empty, protectorless, and unstable— those who are skilled in the yoga of the ultimate truth.
Having prostrated to the Buddha, the knower of the world, and to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Having honored my own teachers and the entire multitude of yogis, and having consulted them,
I shall speak in truth a discourse on the adoption of various paths for the sake of the welfare of those seeking the highest good, so that the Dharma may endure.

Just as one who is terrified abandons four fierce venomous snakes that constantly dwell together in a single basket and cause mutual conflict, even so [one should abandon] those [afflictions] residing within the body.
One should abandon the elements of water, fire, earth, and air;
for just as any one of four highly venomous serpents, if neglected when enraged, leads inevitably to death.
Likewise, one of the four elements inevitably becomes provoked; whichever one it may be, that very same element brings about destruction.
And this can sometimes happen even from a serpent of most terrible venom.
May there be well-being through the mantras and rituals of the great seers;
yet even sages of exalted mind, when bitten at the proper time by a serpent dwelling within the body, have perished. (26.1.9)
There are no venomous serpents in the world that are omnipresent,
nor are there any from which a person does not experience fear;
indeed, apart from the elements, there is no binding of a body.
Wherever they go, the slaughter of living beings is certain.
Furthermore, for those people, there is no fear of death from serpents;
death occurs for someone only from among them [the snakes].
When the body serves as their basis, many gateways to death, which destroys life, arise in the world;
yet even enemies with weapons may attain peace.
Having perceived some virtue [in him], out of a sense of gratitude,
the aggregates (skandhas), though maintained with great effort,
could never be grasped by ungratefulness.
And adversaries who are executioners with raised weapons can be struck down by means of virtues or even by arrows—
even by forces established in righteousness and renowned for their power.
The aggregates cannot be turned back from their own nature.
Having seen another who causes supreme harm, adversaries sometimes repel him, but they do not repel their own side.
Like fires produced by friction from their own source,
the aggregates (skandhas) utterly consume their very own objects on this earth; when the aggregates exist, they become enemies and destroyers.
For fires do not burn trees that have not yet grown;
yet, through dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*), the world goes to destruction even without an enemy, by the power of time, like a lamp at dawn. 26.1.15
By those fools who have constantly and falsely conceived the aggregates as permanent, pleasant, pure, and as a self,
they do not become enemies even on account of that view.
For through association with the wicked, even friends become enemies.
One who is afflicted by the intent to kill may appear equal to a friend; one who is seen to possess virtues may be a true ally, yet in the end, even such a person becomes an enemy.
Subtle through its relish for pleasure and fickle in the enjoyment of sense objects,
the passion of worldly delight burns like a hidden fire;
even here in this very life, the danger caused by that which dwells within becomes manifest.
The enemy does not burn the Dharma nor does it burn knowledge, but it steals away one's lifespan;
first, in this world, the passion for delight burns the strength of the fuel of the mind, and when its maturation is complete, it burns this entire world even in the hereafter. (26.1.18)

Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, it is as if there were four venomous serpents here, fierce in their power and terrible in their poison, cast together into a single basket. Then a man might come who is not of a foolish nature, not of a deluded nature, but of a wise nature; one who desires happiness and is averse to suffering, who desires life and does not desire death, and is averse to dying. Someone would say this to him:”

"O man, these four venomous serpents of fierce splendor and terrible poison have been placed together in a single basket; they must be turned over from time to time, bathed from time to time, fed from time to time, and properly cared for with comfort from time to time."

"O man, when one or another of these four venomous snakes—possessing fierce splendor and terrible poison—should become enraged while they are placed together in a single basket, then you would meet with death or suffering amounting to death. Therefore, O man, do whatever you must do or whatever needs to be done."

[2] Then that man, terrified of those four venomous snakes of fierce splendor and dreadful poison, all placed within a single basket, might flee in any direction whatsoever. Someone would say to him: "O man, these five executioners with raised swords are pursuing you closely from behind; we shall kill you right here at the end of this road, we shall kill you right here at the end of this road! O man, do whatever you must do or whatever needs to be done!"

[3] Then that man, terrified of the four venomous snakes of fierce splendor and dreadful poison all placed within a single basket, and terrified of the five executioners with raised swords, would flee in whichever direction he could. Someone might say to him: "O man, this sixth executioner, an inner-attendant, is following closely behind you; here, having severed your head at its root, I shall cast it down upon the earth."
"Here, having cut off your head at its very root, I shall cast it down upon the earth! O man, do whatever you must do or whatever is to be done by you!"

[4] Then that man, terrified of the four venomous snakes of fierce brilliance and dreadful poison placed within a single basket, and terrified of the five executioners with raised swords, and terrified of the sixth executioner who moves among them, would flee in whatever direction he could. There he might see an empty village; he would enter it. Whatever house he might look into there, he would find it to be entirely empty.

One should perceive it as indeed empty, indeed void, indeed pithless—whatever vessel one might grasp. One would grasp it as indeed empty; one would grasp it as indeed void and indeed pithless. Then someone might say to him: "O man, robbers who plunder villages will come to this deserted village. Lest they deprive you, O man, of your life entirely, do whatever must be done or whatever is to be performed by you, O man."

[5] Then that man, terrified of the four venomous snakes of fierce splendor and dreadful poison all cast into a single basket; terrified of the five executioners with raised swords; terrified of the sixth executioner moving about within; and terrified of the bandits and village-destroying thieves in the deserted village, would flee in whatever direction he could.

There he would see a flood, a great deluge, and a mountain river—deep, swift-flowing, far-reaching, and carrying away all that it encounters. Its near bank would be regarded as full of apprehension, full of danger, and full of peril and terror; whereas its further bank would be secure, auspicious, prosperous, and a source of well-being. Yet, there would be neither boat nor raft for crossing over to the other side, nor even a bridge leading from this shore to the further shore.

It might occur to him: "This is indeed a great flood, a mountain river—deep, swift-flowing, far-reaching, carrying away all that it encounters. Its near bank is regarded as fearful, full of danger, and terrifying; yet its further bank is secure, auspicious, propitious, and a source of well-being. And here there is neither boat nor raft for crossing over to the other side, nor is there a bridge extending from this shore to the one beyond."

And suppose I were to gather together a great quantity of grass, wood, branches, leaves, and straw, and bind them into a raft; having bound the raft, relying upon the raft, and establishing myself upon the raft, I would exert myself with my hands and feet to go against the current. Having reflected thus, he would gather together a great quantity of grass, wood, branches, leaves, and straw, and bind them into a raft;
having bound the raft, relying upon the raft, and establishing himself upon the raft, he exerts himself with his hands and feet to go against the current.

[6] In such and such a way his basket vanishes. The four venomous snakes of fierce splendor and terrible poison, which had been cast into the single basket, vanish. The five executioners with raised swords vanish. The sixth executioner, the one who moves within, vanishes. The empty village vanishes. The thieves who plunder the village vanish. The flood, the great flood, and the mountain river—deep, swift-flowing, far-reaching, and carrying away all that can be carried away—vanish.

The further shore remains far from him—regarded as full of apprehension, full of fear, and full of perilous terrors—while the near shore becomes close to him: secure, auspicious, propitious, and a source of well-being. Having crossed over, having reached the further shore, that brahmin stands on firm ground. [7] Thus, monks, this simile has been employed solely for the purpose of making the meaning known; furthermore, this is the meaning to be understood here.

"O monks, 'casket' (karaṇḍaka) is a designation for this body— this physical, gross body composed of the four great elements, born from the impurity of the mother's and father's kalala, nourished by boiled rice and sour gruel, and subject to constant shaving, bathing, massaging,
scattering, breaking apart, and destruction."

"The four venomous serpents" is a designation for the four elements; namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. Monks, when the earth element is provoked, one may meet death or suffer pain amounting to death; when the water element, the fire element, or the air element is provoked, monks, one may meet death or suffer pain amounting to death.

"The five executioners with raised swords" is a designation for the five aggregates of clinging: namely, the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "The sixth executioner who stalks nearby" is a designation for delight and lust.

"An empty village" is a designation for the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*). That is to say: the internal sense base of the eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the internal sense base of the mind. Monks, when a son of good family contemplates the eye, he contemplates it as truly empty; he contemplates it as truly void; he contemplates it as truly insubstantial and devoid of essence.

“Monks, one grasps at the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind. One grasps at that which is indeed empty; one grasps at that which is indeed void, hollow, and pithless. ‘Bandits, plunderers of the village’—this is a designation for the six external sense bases.

Monks, the eye is struck by agreeable and disagreeable forms; the ear by sounds; the nose by odors; the tongue by tastes; the body by tangibles; and monks, the mind is struck by agreeable and disagreeable mental phenomena.”

"O monks, 'the flood,' 'the great flood'—this is a designation for the four floods: namely, the flood of sensual desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*). O monks, 'the river'—this is a designation for the three cravings (*tṛṣṇā*): namely, craving for sensual pleasures (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*), and craving for the formless (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*). 'The hither shore,' regarded as fearful, regarded as dangerous, and regarded as terrifying and formidable—this is a designation for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*)."

"The far shore, secure, auspicious, prosperous, and a source of well-being"—this is a designation for the *nirvāṇadhātu* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*). "The raft," monks, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path. "Exerting oneself against the current with hands and feet" is a designation for the undertaking of vigor (*vīrya*). "He has crossed over, he has reached the further shore, he stands on firm ground, O Brahmin"—this is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One.

[8] Thus, monks, that which was to be done for the disciples by a teacher who is compassionate, merciful, desirous of their welfare, seeking their benefit, and acting out of pity—that has been done by me. Now, it is for you to do it.

"Monks, these are the forest retreats, the roots of trees, empty huts, mountain clefts, mountain caves, heaps of straw, open spaces, cemeteries, and forest glades—remote lodgings. Meditate, monks; do not be negligent, lest you be full of regret later. This is my instruction. Thus he spoke.
"A village becomes empty, even after having been filled with people; it dwells there for a while, but then gradually becomes empty once more."
But the conjunction with objects in every state is empty;
for it does not have an unreal self, since it does not come into being and then pass away.
[This applies to] memory-based cognition, action, or feeling.
Having seen that everything proceeds from conditions,
the practitioner of yoga perceives neither a self nor anything belonging to a self within the empty sense-faculties. (26.3.2)
"He who sees, touches, smells, hears, and whose there are memory, intellect, and sensation—
he is the self," so they teach, yet they do not point him out.

Just as one searching for a city does not find anything else within its palaces, walls, and houses once it has ceased to exist, so too he did not perceive the Venerable One, who had withdrawn even from his bed and seat.
Having thus reflected upon the self as being merely a conventional designation,
one perceives nothing else within the intellect, the senses, and so forth;
just as there is no city other than its houses and other constituent parts.
There is a city with many foundations, so it is known by tradition;
likewise, there is no other person apart from the senses, yet through conventional usage, a person exists as the locus of action. (26.3.5)
Just as the designation "chariot" occurs when the wheels, the pole,
and so forth have been assembled, so too does the designation "person" occur when the mind and so forth are in a state of combination within this [body].
For when there is grasping at a self and conduct based on falsehood, the world is deluded by hundreds of conditions, seized by the notion of "I" and possessed by the sense of "mine.
Difficult to perceive, difficult to understand, possessing the strength that is hard to overcome, its courses are difficult to fathom.

The objects of the senses— those unwholesome things which destroy virtue and act as enemies to fortitude and wisdom for beings whose minds are distracted, whose darkness is unchecked, and whose senses are unrestrained by passion— are like thieves who plunder the very substance of those who stray from the true path and cause the ruin of their conduct. (26.3.7)

Thieves carry away wealth that possesses only meager virtue; when men commit offenses against the king, they incur neither fear of reproach nor fear of an evil rebirth. But when the wealth of virtue and the like is stolen by the objects of the senses, it is through men's own transgressions.
Severe suffering is obtained by men both here and in the next world when this [life] is taken away.
As long as the sky appears blue like a garment, shimmering as if inlaid with split sapphire, and as long as the sun shines in the heavens with rays resembling the luster of refined gold; || 26.3.8 ||
As long as the moon, garlanded with stars, traverses the earth following the sky with its rays, so long may this teaching of the Lord of Sages shine brilliantly throughout the three worlds.
(26.3.9) "Whatever beings there are here... (26.3.10).
Whatever beings have gathered here, whether dwelling on the earth or in the atmosphere,
may they always maintain loving-kindness toward all creatures and practice the Dharma by day and by night.
